doc.title: Eddie Metz Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, October 3, 2015

title: Freddie Green and Sonny Payne's time
summary: Freddie Green policing the time, and the friction with Sonny Payne heard on Sinatra at the Sands.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: I love your Freddie Green story because I have a story from a bass player, Jimmy Lewis, who was with the small group in the early 50s.
Oh yeah, like the Kansas City Five.
And he basically told the same thing. He says Freddie, he says, if the time starts to get away he would just look at you.

Yeah. He didn’t tolerate it. And yet I heard on Basie records with Sonny Payne near the end of his career with the band, he and Freddie were fighting all the time. You can hear it a couple of times on “Sinatra Live at the Sands.” There’s a couple of times. The set that the Basie band played before Frank Sinatra came out. The dinner set. So you can hear all the silverware clanking and a guy yelling, “waiter.” And maybe the mob guys sitting down front because, you know, Frank was there. “Hey bring me my food” you know. You can hear all that but the Basie band, they are just smoking. But there’s times when Sonny Payne and Freddie were just rubbing each other.
Was Sonny like on the forward side of the beat?
